inputs.need:
I am a consultant radiologist and the reporting lead at Fenwick Cross Hospital. From 11 January 2027 all abdominal and pelvic CT reports in our department will be written in a structured template with fixed headings and pick-lists for key findings, replacing free-text reports. The department agreed the change after surgeons complained that important findings, such as the appendix diameter or the presence of free gas, were missing or buried in long paragraphs.

I would like to run a prospective observational study over the first six months after the switch to find out whether the template is actually used, whether reports contain the key elements that referrers need for the three commonest questions (suspected appendicitis, bowel obstruction and cancer staging), whether reporting takes longer, and whether surgeons and emergency physicians find the reports easier to act on. We will not assign radiologists to use or not use the template; everyone switches on the same day. I can compare with a sample of free-text reports from the six months before the switch, although those reports were not written with the new checklist in mind.

I would like advice on how to define template use (opened, completed, or completed without free-text overrides), how many reports to sample, how to measure completeness fairly for the old free-text reports, and how to ask referrers for their views without a long questionnaire.
inputs.constraints: No extra reporting time for radiologists. Data from the reporting system and a short referrer questionnaire only; no patient contact. One radiology registrar has 3 hours a week for the study from January to July 2027.

records.title: Structured templates for abdominal CT reports and completeness of key findings: a multicentre before-after study
records.authors: Achebe-Lindqvist O, Moreno-Hart P, Takeda-Brennan S
records.abstract: Six hospitals introduced structured templates for abdominal CT and we compared 2,400 reports from six months before with 2,400 from six months after. The proportion of reports containing all pre-specified key elements for the clinical question rose from 64 to 91 percent. Median time from scan completion to report sign-off increased by 2 minutes. Six months after introduction, 88 percent of eligible reports used the template. Improvements were largest for suspected appendicitis and smallest for oncology staging, where free-text additions remained common.

records.title: Radiologist adoption of structured reporting: template use over the first year in one department
records.abstract: We tracked template use for body CT in one department for twelve months after introduction. The template was opened for 94 percent of reports and fully completed for 71 percent; in 23 percent a radiologist overrode the template with free text for at least one section. Use plateaued after four months. Senior radiologists overrode the template more often than junior staff. Radiologists said overrides were most useful for complex or incidental findings. The authors recommend defining use as completion without override when evaluating adoption.

records.title: Structured versus free-text radiology reports: a systematic review of report quality and referrer satisfaction
records.authors: Ibanez-Kowalczyk M, Obi-Sorensen L, Grant-Nakamura A
records.abstract: We included 32 studies comparing structured with free-text radiology reports. Structured reports were more complete in 27 studies and referrer satisfaction was higher in 9 of the 11 studies that measured it. No study measured patient outcomes. Most studies were before-after comparisons in single departments, and completeness checklists were often designed with the template, which may favour structured reports. We found no evidence that structured reporting increased reporting errors. Few studies reported how often radiologists overrode templates, so adoption could rarely be judged alongside completeness.

records.title: What referring clinicians want from CT reports for suspected appendicitis: a preference study
records.abstract: We asked 146 surgeons and emergency physicians to choose between pairs of CT reports for suspected appendicitis that differed in structure, length and content. Clinicians valued an explicit statement of the appendix diameter, the presence or absence of free fluid and gas, and a clear one-line impression. Long reports reduced perceived usefulness even when complete. Emergency physicians valued the impression line more than surgeons did, while surgeons valued explicit measurements more. Responses came from three hospitals with established free-text reporting, so preferences may shift once clinicians are used to structured reports.

records.title: Measuring completeness of historic free-text reports against a new structured checklist: rater agreement
records.abstract: Two radiologists rated 300 free-text abdominal CT reports against a 12-item checklist written for a new structured template. Agreement was good (kappa 0.72). Completeness was underestimated when elements were implied rather than stated, for example when a normal appendix was described without a diameter. Applying a rule that counted an element as present when it was stated or clearly implied raised measured completeness of free-text reports by 9 percentage points. The authors recommend pre-specifying such a rule before any before-after comparison.

records.title: Reporting time with structured templates in body CT: a time-stamp analysis
records.abstract: We analysed time stamps for 9,800 body CT reports before and after the introduction of structured templates. Median active reporting time increased by 1.4 minutes in the first month and returned to the pre-template level by the fourth month. Oncology staging reports remained about one minute longer throughout. Radiologists who had helped design the template returned to baseline faster. Time stamps do not capture interruptions, so active reporting time may be overestimated. Turnaround from scan to sign-off, which also depends on worklist order, changed less than active reporting time.

response.synthesis: Six retrieved records, appraised at abstract level. Structured templates were followed by more complete reports in a multicentre study (64 to 91 percent) and in most studies in a systematic review, with higher referrer satisfaction where measured. Adoption plateaus after about four months, with overrides common among senior radiologists, and reporting time rises briefly before returning to baseline. Historic free-text reports need a stated-or-implied rule to be compared fairly.
response.gradeRationale: Consistent completeness gains across a multicentre study and a systematic review of 32 studies, downgraded for before-after designs and checklists designed with templates; certainty for reporting time and referrer views is lower.
response.summary: Six retrieved records appraised; three claims recorded; overall certainty moderate for completeness.

response.reading: The template can only improve decisions if it is used as intended, so adoption is the first link: opened, completed and not overridden. Completeness then determines whether referrers find the elements they need, while reporting time is the cost radiologists pay. Historic free-text reports are a fragile comparison unless implied elements are counted fairly.

response.procedures: Each month the registrar samples 25 reports per index question (75 a month) from the reporting system by random number, extracts template status (opened, completed, overridden) and rates key elements against the checklist. response.sampleSize: To estimate completeness near 90 percent within 5 percentage points (95 percent confidence), about 140 reports per index question are needed over the study (1.96 squared times 0.09 divided by 0.0025, about 138). The historic reference of 150 reports (50 per question) estimates a completeness near 65 percent within about 13 points per question.

response.title: Adoption, completeness and reporting time after the introduction of structured abdominal CT reports: a prospective observational study
response.abstract: Objective: to describe adoption of a structured template, completeness of key elements for three index questions, reporting time and referrer views in the six months after introduction. Design: prospective observational study with rated free-text reports from the previous six months as context. Results will follow data collection.
response.introduction: Structured reports are more complete in most studies, but adoption plateaus and overrides are common, and historic comparisons can be unfair to free-text reports.
response.methods: Each month 25 reports per index question are sampled at random and rated against a fixed checklist; template use is recorded as opened, completed and completed without override. Historic free-text reports are rated with a stated-or-clearly-implied rule fixed in advance. Active reporting time comes from system time stamps and referrer views from a five-item questionnaire at months 3 and 6.
response.results: Data collection starts on 2027-01-11. The report will give completeness by index question with intervals, monthly run charts of adoption and reporting time, and referrer scores.
response.discussion: To be written. The comparison with historic reports will be treated as context, not as an effect estimate.
response.limitations: No concurrent comparison; the checklist was designed with the template.
response.conclusion: To be written after six months of data.
